query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a ceramic or refractory metal coating to boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment will improve their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by forming a protective barrier that prevents direct contact between the molten aluminum and the boride-based components.
generation.material_initial_state: boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment
generation.intervention: applying a ceramic or refractory metal coating
generation.structural_mediator: protective ceramic or refractory metal coating
generation.mechanism: formation of a protective barrier preventing direct contact between molten aluminum and boride-based components
generation.predicted_outcome: improved resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by at least 30% relative to uncoated components
generation.boundary: operating temperature of the hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment
generation.uncertainty: the actual improvement in corrosion resistance may vary depending on the specific ceramic or refractory metal coating used and the operating conditions of the equipment

falsification_experiment.design: controlled experiment comparing the corrosion resistance of coated and uncoated boride-based components in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the corrosion rate of the coated components is not at least 30% lower than that of the uncoated components, the hypothesis is falsified

Mn also shows a rapid evaporation effect during melting processes; hence, in our study, this element was replaced by Mo, which could improve the resistance to high temperatures []. Co–Cr–Mo alloy is widely used for manufacturing of vanes and gas turbines due to its excellent fatigue behavior and wear resistance [,,,]. In such alloys, molybdenum has a beneficial effect on passivation capacity, contributing to the formation of a protective surface layer that allows pitting corrosion to be limited [,]. Studies were conducted to estimate the effects on the microstructure and properties of alloys with different Mo contents [,,]. Such alloys have been designed for the manufacture of furnace casings and chemical tanks used in high-temperature and corrosion conditions [], for components used in the geothermal industry [,], or to obtain high-performance coatings [].

ZrC can effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating, and the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating increases with increasing ZrC content. The annual corrosion rate of the 04ZrC coating in a 1 mol/L NaCl solution is only 21.5% of that of the HEA. Consequently, the addition of ZrC to the FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy alloy coating holds promise for applications in corrosion resistance, particularly in oceanic environments.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr2O3), alumina (Al2O3) or silica (SiO2) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation. However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components,. The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.
